title: Hilt
scopeHtml: Scope: Hilt's component hierarchy and scopes, entry points, ViewModel/WorkManager/Compose integration, testing, multi-module, build cost, migration from Dagger, scope leaks and common errors. Versions referenced: Hilt/Dagger 2.57.x per the Android docs (dagger.dev setup page showed 2.60.x; verify the latest), androidx.hilt 1.x, KSP.

questions.promptHtml: What does Hilt give you over plain Dagger on Android, and what are the minimum annotations needed to get a screen injected?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know Hilt is Dagger plus a fixed set of Android components, scopes and bindings, not a different engine.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Hilt is a Dagger layer that predefines the component hierarchy for Android (Singleton, ActivityRetained, ViewModel, Activity, Fragment, View, Service), the matching scopes, and default bindings like Application and @ApplicationContext. I annotate the Application with @HiltAndroidApp, each Activity or Fragment with @AndroidEntryPoint, tell Hilt how to build things with @Inject constructors or @Module @InstallIn, and it does all the component wiring I would have hand-written in Dagger.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
In raw Dagger you write components, subcomponents, builders, and call component.inject(this) in every framework class because the OS constructs Activities, not you. Hilt generates that. At compile time Hilt generates Dagger components for each entry point and Dagger still validates the whole graph, so you keep compile-time safety and no reflection at runtime.

@HiltAndroidApp  -> generates Hilt_App base class + SingletonComponent
@AndroidEntryPoint -> generates Hilt_MainActivity, ActivityComponent injection in onCreate
@Module @InstallIn(X::class) -> contributes bindings to component X (and its children)

Bindings are unscoped by default: each request makes a new instance. The Hilt Gradle plugin rewrites the superclass of annotated classes to the generated Hilt_ class, so you write class App : Application() and not Hilt_App.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@HiltAndroidApp
class App : Application()

@AndroidEntryPoint
class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    @Inject lateinit var analytics: Analytics   // not private
}

class Analytics @Inject constructor(private val api: AnalyticsApi)

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object NetModule {
    @Provides @Singleton
    fun api(client: OkHttpClient): AnalyticsApi = Retrofit.Builder()
        .baseUrl("https://example.com/").client(client).build().create()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting @InstallIn: the module is silently ignored for graph purposes and you get MissingBinding.
  • private injected fields: compile error.
  • Annotating a composable: composables are not entry points; annotate the host ComponentActivity and use hiltViewModel().
  • Activity must extend ComponentActivity (for example AppCompatActivity).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Hilt use reflection? → No, it is generated code verified at compile time by Dagger.
  2. Can Hilt and Dagger coexist? → Yes; custom Dagger components can be children of Hilt components.
  3. Why can't I add my own component between Activity and Singleton? → Hilt fixes the hierarchy; @DefineComponent can add custom ones but cannot insert into the standard chain.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists annotations. The senior answer explains that Hilt trades flexibility for a standard graph shape, which lets teams share modules and tooling, and names what you give up (custom hierarchy, retained fragments).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams adopting Hilt on a legacy Dagger app hit "custom component does not map to the Hilt hierarchy" first, which drives the migration plan (see the migration question).

questions.promptHtml: Draw Hilt's component hierarchy and state when each component is created and destroyed.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Lifecycle mapping is the root of every scope bug.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SingletonComponent is the root, tied to the Application. Under it sit ActivityRetainedComponent and ServiceComponent. Under ActivityRetainedComponent sit ActivityComponent and ViewModelComponent. Fragment is under Activity, View under Fragment or Activity. A child can see every binding of its ancestors, never the reverse.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SingletonComponent                  App onCreate -> process death
 |- ServiceComponent                Service onCreate -> onDestroy
 `- ActivityRetainedComponent       first Activity onCreate -> last Activity onDestroy (survives rotation)
     |- ViewModelComponent          ViewModel created -> onCleared
     `- ActivityComponent           Activity onCreate -> onDestroy
         `- FragmentComponent       Fragment onAttach -> onDestroy
             `- ViewComponent       View construction -> destroyed

Per the official table: ActivityRetainedComponent lives across configuration changes, so it starts at the first onCreate and ends at the final onDestroy. BroadcastReceivers have no component; they are injected from SingletonComponent. Default bindings: Singleton and ActivityRetained give Application; ViewModelComponent gives SavedStateHandle; ActivityComponent gives Application and Activity; ServiceComponent gives Application and Service.

Direction rule: a binding in a child can depend on any ancestor binding. A @Singleton class cannot inject @ActivityScoped things. ViewModelComponent is a sibling of ActivityComponent, so a ViewModel cannot inject Activity bindings (this is what stops Activity leaks into ViewModels).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// compile error: Singleton cannot depend on a shorter-lived scope
@Singleton
class Repo @Inject constructor(private val activity: Activity)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking ActivityRetained dies on rotation. It does not.
  • Assuming ViewModelComponent can see Activity.
  • Forgetting that one Hilt ActivityComponent definition serves all activities; the instances differ per activity.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why no component for BroadcastReceiver? → Receivers are short-lived and injected from Singleton.
  2. Which component is destroyed on process death? → All; scopes are per process, not persisted.
  3. Where does SavedStateHandle come from? → ViewModelComponent default binding.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: recite the diagram. Senior: derives why the ViewModel/Activity sibling relationship exists and uses it to decide where state may live.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An Activity-typed dependency pulled into a @Singleton is the classic leak that this hierarchy is designed to make a compile error.

questions.promptHtml: Bindings in Hilt are unscoped by default. What does that mean, and when should you actually add a scope?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Over-scoping everything with @Singleton is the most common Hilt smell.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Unscoped means every injection site gets a new instance. A scope makes Hilt create one instance per component instance and keep it in memory until that component dies. I add a scope only when the object holds state that must be shared, needs synchronization, or has been measured as expensive to create.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Scoped bindings are held by the component in a DoubleCheck provider (lazy, thread-safe, one instance). The official guidance: scoping can be costly because the object lives until the component is destroyed, so minimize it. A scope annotation on a class must match the component where it is installed; @Singleton class used from @InstallIn(ActivityComponent) is a compile error.

Good @Singleton: OkHttpClient, Room database, an in-memory cache, a rate limiter. Bad: stateless mappers, use cases, thin repositories wrapping a singleton DAO. Unscoped stateless objects are cheap and avoid retention.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class PriceFormatter @Inject constructor()          // unscoped, stateless

@Singleton
class SessionCache @Inject constructor()            // shared mutable state => scoped

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• @Singleton on every repository "for performance".
  • Scoping a class that holds a View/Context.
  • Expecting a scoped binding to be a global object: it is per component instance.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is @Singleton thread-safe creation? → Yes, double-checked provider; your own state still needs thread safety.
  2. Does a scoped binding start at app start? → No, lazily on first request.
  3. Scoped vs object? → A Hilt scope is replaceable in tests and lifecycle-bound; object is neither.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Singleton means one instance". Senior: names the cost model (retention until component death) and lists criteria for scoping.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Apps with 300+ singleton bindings pay graph memory and retain stale user data after logout (see the logout leak scenario).

questions.promptHtml: Compare @ActivityScoped, @ActivityRetainedScoped, @ViewModelScoped and @Singleton. How would you choose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand lifetimes and sharing semantics rather than names.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Singleton lives for the process. ActivityRetained lives from first Activity create to last Activity destroy, surviving rotation, shared by everything in that activity. ActivityScoped dies and is recreated on rotation. ViewModelScoped gives one instance per ViewModel and is shared only among the dependencies of that one ViewModel.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Scope Lifetime Shared with Survives rotation
@Singleton process everyone yes
@ActivityRetainedScoped activity task instance all VMs/fragments in that activity yes
@ViewModelScoped one ViewModel only that ViewModel's deps yes (with the VM)
@ActivityScoped Activity instance activity-level objects no

Per the Android docs, if one instance must be shared across multiple ViewModels, use @ActivityRetainedScoped or @Singleton; two ViewModels asking for a @ViewModelScoped type get different instances. In a single-activity app @ActivityRetainedScoped behaves almost like @Singleton except it is dropped when the activity finishes (the Mercari write-up makes the same point). Choose the shortest scope that satisfies sharing: per-VM helper (paginator, debouncer) -> ViewModelScoped; per-session coordination -> ActivityRetained; app-wide -> Singleton.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@ViewModelScoped
class SearchDebouncer @Inject constructor()

@HiltViewModel
class SearchVM @Inject constructor(
    private val debouncer: SearchDebouncer,   // same instance in all deps of THIS VM
    private val repo: SearchRepo,             // repo also gets this VM's debouncer
) : ViewModel()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using @ActivityScoped for something a ViewModel needs: VM cannot see it.
  • Assuming @ViewModelScoped is shared across screens.
  • Assuming ActivityRetained is per-screen in a single-activity app.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a ViewModel inject an @ActivityRetainedScoped object? → Yes, ancestor binding.
  2. Can an @ActivityRetainedScoped class inject a @ViewModelScoped one? → No, child to parent is not allowed.
  3. How do you get a per-screen scope across several ViewModels? → Share a parent ViewModel via nav-graph scoping, or a custom @DefineComponent (see the design question).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: orders them by lifetime. Senior: reasons about sharing semantics, rotation, and the single-activity collapse of Retained vs Singleton.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams used @Singleton "wizard state" that leaked data between runs of a checkout flow; shorter scope fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: @Binds vs @Provides in a Hilt module: when do you use which, and why is @Binds preferred for interfaces?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic Dagger literacy plus awareness of generated-code cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: @Binds maps an implementation to an interface with no body, in an abstract class or interface module. @Provides runs real code, for things I don't own or must build with a builder. @Binds generates less code and no module instance, so I prefer it whenever it fits.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: @Provides methods are real methods Dagger calls; the module must be instantiable (Kotlin object fixes that). @Binds is an alias edge in the graph: no factory class is generated for the method itself. A module can't mix @Binds (abstract) and instance @Provides unless the @Provides are in a companion object marked @Module or placed in a separate module.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
abstract class RepoModule {
    @Binds abstract fun repo(impl: OrdersRepoImpl): OrdersRepo
}

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object DbModule {
    @Provides @Singleton
    fun db(@ApplicationContext c: Context): AppDb =
        Room.databaseBuilder(c, AppDb::class.java, "app.db").build()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Scoping the @Binds target class and the binding method inconsistently (scope the method or the class, not confuse both).
  • @Provides returning the impl type then needing a second binding for the interface.
  • Installing in the wrong component and getting MissingBinding in a different one.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why object modules? → No instance allocation; static calls.
  2. Can @Binds take a scope? → Yes, the scope goes on the @Binds method.
  3. How do you bind a Lazy? → Inject Lazy<T>/Provider<T>, no extra binding needed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: syntax. Senior: generated-code difference, module mixing rule, scope placement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Large modules of @Provides that merely return impls inflate kapt/KSP output and build time.

questions.promptHtml: How does @HiltViewModel work, and how does hiltViewModel() get the right instance in Compose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests that you know the factory mechanics and the scoping-to-back-stack-entry behavior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: @HiltViewModel plus @Inject constructor makes Hilt generate a multibinding of ViewModel classes into a map and a ViewModelProvider.Factory. An @AndroidEntryPoint host supplies that factory as its default one, so viewModels() or hiltViewModel() just work. In Navigation Compose, hiltViewModel() uses the current back stack entry as the owner, so the ViewModel is scoped to that destination.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The ViewModel is built inside a ViewModelComponent (child of ActivityRetained), which provides SavedStateHandle as a default binding. Hence a Hilt ViewModel can inject Singleton, ActivityRetained and ViewModelScoped bindings, never Activity or Fragment. Arguments from navigation arrive through SavedStateHandle (type-safe routes can be decoded with toRoute() in Navigation 2.8+; verify against your version). hiltViewModel() comes from androidx.hilt:hilt-lifecycle-viewmodel-compose (docs show 1.3.0; verify) and requires the host Activity to be @AndroidEntryPoint.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@HiltViewModel
class DetailVM @Inject constructor(
    savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle,
    private val repo: ItemRepo,
) : ViewModel() {
    private val id: String = checkNotNull(savedStateHandle["id"])
}

@Composable
fun DetailRoute() {
    val vm: DetailVM = hiltViewModel()   // owner = current NavBackStackEntry
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting @AndroidEntryPoint on the host Activity: runtime crash about missing factory.
  • Injecting Context unqualified (not available; use @ApplicationContext).
  • Calling hiltViewModel() outside a NavHost expecting per-destination behavior.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't a Hilt ViewModel take an Activity? → ViewModelComponent has no Activity binding by design (leak safety).
  2. How do two screens share a ViewModel? → hiltViewModel(parentBackStackEntry) of a shared nav graph.
  3. Is the ViewModel constructor called on rotation? → No, the same instance is retained.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "annotate and use hiltViewModel". Senior: explains component, factory, owner and the sibling rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Crash "Hilt ViewModel factory missing" after adding a second Activity without @AndroidEntryPoint.

questions.promptHtml: How do you pass a runtime argument (for example a userId) into a Hilt-injected ViewModel, and which options exist?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Runtime parameters plus DI is a classic friction point.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Easiest: read it from SavedStateHandle. When I want a typed constructor parameter, I use @HiltViewModel(assistedFactory = ...) with @AssistedInject, @Assisted for the runtime value and an @AssistedFactory; in Compose I pass a creationCallback to hiltViewModel.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: @Assisted parameters are not in the graph; the generated factory takes them and fills the rest from Hilt. The docs show the pattern with a nested @AssistedFactory interface and @HiltViewModel(assistedFactory = MyViewModel.Factory::class). The hiltViewModel creation callback overload takes the factory (check the exact signature in your hilt-lifecycle-viewmodel-compose version; verify). Avoid passing arguments that already live in the route; SavedStateHandle survives process death, a captured assisted value only survives if re-supplied by the caller.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@HiltViewModel(assistedFactory = ProfileVM.Factory::class)
class ProfileVM @AssistedInject constructor(
    @Assisted private val userId: String,
    private val repo: UserRepo,
) : ViewModel() {
    @AssistedFactory interface Factory { fun create(userId: String): ProfileVM }
}

@Composable
fun ProfileRoute(userId: String) {
    val vm = hiltViewModel<ProfileVM, ProfileVM.Factory>(
        creationCallback = { factory -> factory.create(userId) }
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mixing plain @Inject and @AssistedInject constructors.
  • Same-typed assisted params without identifiers: use @Assisted("a")/@Assisted("b").
  • Key reuse: the VM is keyed by owner, so a different userId on the same entry returns the old VM.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not a custom ViewModelProvider.Factory? → Loses compile-time validation and Hilt wiring.
  2. Process death? → Pull ids from SavedStateHandle if the value must survive.
  3. Same screen, two ids in the back stack? → Distinct back stack entries give distinct VMs; same entry does not.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: assisted factory syntax. Senior: weighs SavedStateHandle vs assisted, plus the stale-VM-per-key trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A profile screen kept showing user A after navigating to user B from the same entry.

questions.promptHtml: What is a Hilt @EntryPoint, when do you need one, and what is @EarlyEntryPoint?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know how to reach the graph from code Hilt does not construct.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An entry point is an interface annotated @EntryPoint @InstallIn(X) that exposes bindings from component X to code Hilt doesn't manage: a ContentProvider, a third-party class, a custom Dagger component. I fetch it with EntryPointAccessors.fromApplication/fromActivity. @EarlyEntryPoint is a test-only escape hatch for access before the singleton component exists in tests.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Entry points are the boundary between managed and unmanaged code. The accessor must match the component in @InstallIn: Singleton -> fromApplication(context.applicationContext, ...), Activity -> fromActivity. Per the docs, @EarlyEntryPoint is only needed when Application.onCreate() or ContentProvider.onCreate() calls the entry point in a Hilt test; it must be installed in SingletonComponent, be accessed with EarlyEntryPoints.get(), and does not share state with the test's singleton component (so not even @Singleton bindings are shared, and @BindValue isn't visible). In production it behaves like a normal entry point.

Prefer constructor injection and @AndroidEntryPoint first. Entry points are service-locator-ish: use them at edges only.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@EntryPoint @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
interface SyncEntryPoint { fun syncEngine(): SyncEngine }

class SyncProvider : ContentProvider() {
    override fun onCreate(): Boolean = true
    override fun query(...): Cursor? {
        val ep = EntryPointAccessors.fromApplication(
            context!!.applicationContext, SyncEntryPoint::class.java)
        return ep.syncEngine().cursor()
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling an entry point from ContentProvider.onCreate() (runs before Application.onCreate(), singleton may not exist).
  • Passing an Activity context to a Singleton entry point accessor mismatch.
  • Using entry points as a general backdoor, recreating a service locator.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does ContentProvider.onCreate break? → Providers initialize before Application.onCreate; use lazy access in query/insert or App Startup.
  2. Can entry points be scoped? → They expose bindings; scope comes from the underlying binding.
  3. How do you migrate a Dagger component's exposed getters? → Convert to an entry point (see migration).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "for classes Hilt doesn't support". Senior: boundary mindset, timing traps, test implications.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Init-order crashes from providers that touched the graph in onCreate.

questions.promptHtml: How do you inject dependencies into a Worker and a Service with Hilt? What can go wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Background components are constructed by the framework, which is where many DI setups fail.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Service: annotate with @AndroidEntryPoint and inject fields; it gets a ServiceComponent. Worker: @HiltWorker with @AssistedInject, @Assisted Context and WorkerParameters, plus a HiltWorkerFactory set in the app's Configuration.Provider, and the default WorkManager initializer removed from the manifest.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: WorkManager instantiates workers reflectively through a WorkerFactory. HiltWorkerFactory knows generated assisted factories. The docs require androidx.hilt:hilt-work (1.0.0 shown) and a ksp("androidx.hilt:hilt-compiler:...") processor in addition to the Hilt compiler (version shown 1.4.0 in the docs I read; verify). Only @Singleton or unscoped bindings are allowed in Workers (no Activity or ViewModel scopes because Workers outlive screens). If the default WorkManagerInitializer remains, WorkManager initializes with the default factory and fails with Could not instantiate ...Worker (no-arg constructor).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@HiltWorker
class UploadWorker @AssistedInject constructor(
    @Assisted ctx: Context,
    @Assisted params: WorkerParameters,
    private val repo: UploadRepo,
) : CoroutineWorker(ctx, params) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result = repo.flush().let { Result.success() }
}

@HiltAndroidApp
class App : Application(), Configuration.Provider {
    @Inject lateinit var factory: HiltWorkerFactory
    override val workManagerConfiguration: Configuration
        get() = Configuration.Builder().setWorkerFactory(factory).build()
}
<provider android:name="androidx.startup.InitializationProvider"
    android:authorities="${applicationId}.androidx-startup" tools:node="merge">
    <meta-data android:name="androidx.work.WorkManagerInitializer"
        tools:node="remove" />
</provider>

(Property vs method form of Configuration.Provider differs by WorkManager version; verify.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Removing the whole InitializationProvider and breaking other startup initializers.
  • Missing androidx.hilt:hilt-compiler: worker never gets a factory.
  • Injecting @ActivityScoped things into a worker.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why @AssistedInject? → Context and params are provided by WorkManager at runtime.
  2. WorkManager used before graph ready? → Config is lazy; workerFactory field injected in super.onCreate().
  3. BroadcastReceiver? → Injected from SingletonComponent; @AndroidEntryPoint works, beware async goAsync work.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: the annotations. Senior: init order, manifest merge hazards, scope restrictions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Release builds crashed on jobs after a manifest-merge tool re-added the default initializer.

questions.promptHtml: Show how to inject different CoroutineDispatchers or two OkHttpClients, and how to avoid ambiguity bugs.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Qualifier hygiene and testability of dispatchers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I define custom @Qualifier annotations (@IoDispatcher, @AuthClient), annotate every provider and every injection site, and also qualify the "default" one rather than leaving one unqualified. For Android contexts I use Hilt's @ApplicationContext and @ActivityContext.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A binding key = type + qualifier. Two @Provides of the same type with no qualifier is a duplicate binding error; with one unqualified and one qualified it compiles but injecting without a qualifier silently picks the unqualified one, which the docs call error-prone. Dispatchers should be injected so tests can swap them with StandardTestDispatcher. Use @Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Qualifier @Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY) annotation class IoDispatcher
@Qualifier @Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY) annotation class DefaultDispatcher

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object DispatcherModule {
    @IoDispatcher @Provides fun io(): CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO
    @DefaultDispatcher @Provides fun default(): CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Default
}

class Repo @Inject constructor(@IoDispatcher private val io: CoroutineDispatcher)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the qualifier at the injection site (Kotlin: use @field:IoDispatcher for field injection in some cases; constructor params are fine).
  • One qualifier for two meanings.
  • @Named("io") strings: no compile-time typo safety.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. @ApplicationContext vs @ActivityContext? → Process-long vs activity-long; never keep the latter in a Singleton.
  2. Qualifier on @Binds? → Yes, on the method.
  3. How do qualifiers show in error text? → Printed as part of the key.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: uses @Named. Senior: custom qualifiers, qualify all variants, dispatcher injection for tests.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A background call went through the authenticated client by accident and leaked tokens to a third-party host.

questions.promptHtml: How would you use Hilt multibindings (@IntoSet, @IntoMap) for a plug-in style feature registry across modules?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows how multi-module apps compose features without the app module knowing each one.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each feature module installs a module with @Binds @IntoSet (or @IntoMap @StringKey) into SingletonComponent; the consumer injects Set<Initializer> or Map<String, Provider<Handler>>. Hilt merges all contributions in the app's graph at compile time, so adding a feature is adding a module.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Contributions come from every Hilt module on the app's classpath (aggregated by the Hilt plugin/aggregating task). Order in a Set is not guaranteed. Use Provider<T> values in maps to avoid eager construction. Empty multibinding needs @Multibinds declaration or Dagger reports a missing binding. Tests can add with @BindValueIntoSet.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface StartupTask { fun run() }

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
abstract class FeatureAModule {
    @Binds @IntoSet abstract fun task(t: FeatureAInit): StartupTask
}

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
abstract class EmptyModule { @Multibinds abstract fun tasks(): Set<StartupTask> }

class Bootstrapper @Inject constructor(private val tasks: Set<@JvmSuppressWildcards StartupTask>)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Missing @JvmSuppressWildcards on Kotlin Set<Foo> or Map<K, V> causing MissingBinding with ? extends.
  • Relying on ordering.
  • Eagerly constructing everything at startup through a Set.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Duplicate map keys? → Compile error.
  2. Per-feature lazy creation? → Map<String, Provider<T>>.
  3. Replace one contribution in a test? → @UninstallModules or @TestInstallIn the module, since you cannot remove a single entry.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: syntax. Senior: Kotlin wildcard trap, startup cost, and test replacement limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: App Startup-like registries via multibinding made cold start 150 ms slower until initializers were made Provider-based.

questions.promptHtml: Compare @TestInstallIn, @UninstallModules with a nested module, and @BindValue. When do you use each, and when do you skip Hilt in tests?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Test design and build-time awareness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Unit tests construct classes directly and don't need Hilt. For integration/UI tests, @TestInstallIn(replaces = ...) replaces a production module for all tests in that source set, and is recommended. @UninstallModules plus a nested module or @BindValue replaces for a single test class but creates new components and slows builds.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Setup (Android docs, Hilt 2.57.x shown): @HiltAndroidTest, HiltAndroidRule with order = 0, HiltTestApplication via a custom AndroidJUnitRunner.newApplication or Robolectric @Config(application = ...), and hilt-android-testing plus kspAndroidTest/kspTest of the compiler. Call hiltRule.inject() before using @Inject fields. Compose tests need a @AndroidEntryPoint HiltTestActivity in the debug/androidTest manifest. Each test gets fresh components, so singleton state does not leak between tests unless you use @EarlyEntryPoint.

@TestInstallIn  -> one global replacement, shared components, fast
@UninstallModules + nested/BindValue -> per class; extra component generation per class

You cannot @UninstallModules a @TestInstallIn module, nor modules without @InstallIn.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Module @TestInstallIn(components = [SingletonComponent::class], replaces = [NetworkModule::class])
object FakeNetworkModule {
    @Provides @Singleton fun api(): Api = FakeApi()
}

@HiltAndroidTest
class FeedScreenTest {
    @get:Rule(order = 0) val hilt = HiltAndroidRule(this)
    @get:Rule(order = 1) val compose = createAndroidComposeRule<HiltTestActivity>()
    @Inject lateinit var api: Api
    @Before fun setUp() = hilt.inject()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrong rule order: components not ready.
  • Replacing modules in the wrong component.
  • Overusing @UninstallModules and exploding test build time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not use Hilt in unit tests? → Constructor injection means you can call constructors.
  2. Test-only DataStore/dispatcher? → Provide through test module; inject dispatcher.
  3. Parallel tests sharing state? → Each test has its own components, but any object or static state is still shared.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: replaces a module. Senior: compares speed, scope, ordering, and when not to use Hilt.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: CI instrumentation time doubled after 40 classes switched to @UninstallModules.

questions.promptHtml: How does Hilt work across Gradle modules with an api/impl split? Where do @InstallIn modules and @Binds live, and what must the app module see?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Hilt's global-graph assumption collides with strict module boundaries.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The public :feature:x:api module holds interfaces only. The :impl module holds the implementation and a @Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent) with @Binds. Hilt generates components in the module that compiles @HiltAndroidApp, which must have every Hilt module and @Inject class in its transitive classpath, so the app module depends on every :impl. Consumers depend only on :api.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The official docs state: because Hilt's code generation needs access to all Gradle modules that use Hilt, the module compiling the Application must have all Hilt modules and constructor-injected classes in its transitive dependencies. With implementation edges, Dagger processing in the app module may not see types of transitive implementation deps; the options are api edges (leaks compile classpath, hurts incrementality), or Hilt's aggregating task (enableAggregatingTask, default on in current plugin per the dagger.dev setup page; it replaced enableExperimentalClasspathAggregation), which collects the Hilt metadata so implementation deps suffice.

:app (HiltAndroidApp) -> :feature:cart:impl -> :feature:cart:api
                      -> :feature:search:impl -> :feature:search:api
:feature:cart:impl -> :feature:search:api   (never :search:impl)

Rules: bind interface to impl inside the impl module, so no one else can name the impl. Leaf modules apply the Hilt plugin and compiler; only the app needs @HiltAndroidApp. Library modules cannot define @AndroidEntryPoint roots without being aggregated by the app.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :feature:cart:impl
@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
internal abstract class CartBindings {
    @Binds abstract fun cart(impl: CartRepoImpl): CartRepo   // CartRepo lives in :api
}

Module classes can be internal only if generated code can see them; Hilt handles Kotlin internal modules in its generated code but verify with your KSP/Hilt version.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• App module forgets to depend on a new :impl: runtime-less compile error "MissingBinding" at the app.
  • Making :impl visible to siblings via api, destroying boundaries.
  • Duplicate bindings when two modules both @Binds the same api type.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you enforce that no feature depends on another's impl? → Convention plugin plus Konsist/dependency-guard check.
  2. Why not have the app write bindings? → Defeats encapsulation and creates a god module.
  3. Can a library module have its own component? → Custom Dagger component as an entry-point child, with trade-offs (see the SDK question).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "put modules in each feature". Senior: classpath requirements, aggregation, api edge cost, and enforcement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A new feature merged without the app dependency passed unit tests but failed the release app build on MissingBinding.

questions.promptHtml: Why can Hilt slow down builds, and what can you do about it (KSP vs kapt, aggregating task, graph size)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers own the CI time budget.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Hilt runs annotation processing in every module with Hilt annotations, and the app module runs the heaviest pass (component generation and whole-graph validation). kapt generates Java stubs first, so it is slow. Move to KSP, keep the aggregating task enabled, avoid api leaks, shrink the app module, and use build scans to measure.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Costs: (1) kapt stub generation per module; KSP avoids stubs. Hilt supports KSP (docs show ksp("com.google.dagger:hilt-android-compiler:...")). With kapt, correctErrorTypes = true. (2) Whole-graph validation in the app module reruns whenever any binding in any module changes. (3) Classpath aggregation: the older enableExperimentalClasspathAggregation can increase build time and is slated for removal; the aggregating task makes processors isolating for better incremental builds. (4) @UninstallModules in tests generates extra components.

Measurements to take: ./gradlew :app:assembleDebug --scan, check kspDebugKotlin/hiltAggregateDepsDebug/kaptDebugKotlin task durations and cache hits; compare clean vs incremental after one-line change in a leaf.

Mitigations: KSP everywhere (some libs like older Room/Dagger plugins may still need kapt; verify), enable configuration and build cache, put @Provides in object modules, prefer @Binds, reduce @InstallIn(SingletonComponent) giant modules, avoid mega-app module by keeping logic in features.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
plugins {
    id("com.google.devtools.ksp")
    id("com.google.dagger.hilt.android")
}
dependencies {
    implementation("com.google.dagger:hilt-android:<ver>")
    ksp("com.google.dagger:hilt-android-compiler:<ver>")
}
hilt { enableAggregatingTask = true }  // default; shown for clarity

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mixing kapt and KSP for Hilt compiler in the same module.
  • Blaming Hilt without measuring; Room or Moshi codegen may dominate.
  • Turning dependencies into api to "fix" Dagger errors.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. KSP2 compatibility? → Verify against your Hilt and Kotlin versions.
  2. Does Hilt affect runtime speed? → Little; graph is generated code, singleton creation lazy.
  3. Can the graph validation be skipped in dev? → Not safely; reduce graph or module count instead.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use KSP". Senior: identifies tasks, measures, explains why app module is the choke point.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Incremental builds of 4 minutes after one-line changes dropped after kapt to KSP plus removing api edges (see the build-time scenario).

questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate a large Dagger 2 app to Hilt incrementally, and what do you do with components that do not fit Hilt's hierarchy?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real apps rarely start on Hilt.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Map your components to Hilt's, migrate Application and the singleton component first, then Activities, then Fragments, building between steps; Hilt and non-Hilt classes can coexist. Hilt cannot insert components into its hierarchy, so oddball components stay as manual Dagger components under a Hilt parent through entry points or @InstallIn subcomponents.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the dagger.dev migration guide: (1) install existing modules in SingletonComponent, possibly via a temporary aggregator module; (2) move interfaces your component extended into an @EntryPoint in SingletonComponent; (3) switch scopes to @Singleton or use scope aliases; (4) replace component arguments with Hilt's predefined bindings; (5) annotate @HiltAndroidApp and delete the component code; keep dagger.android until every dagger.android Activity/Fragment is migrated. Hilt Activities require a Hilt Application, Hilt Fragments a Hilt Activity. Pitfalls: Hilt uses a single shared Activity component, so bindings that differ per Activity conflict or must be generalized to FragmentActivity; retained fragments are unsupported, move state to a ViewModel.

Custom components: keep as manual Dagger with component dependencies on an entry point, or install a subcomponent into the Hilt parent. @DefineComponent can create a new child (for example a logged-in user scope) with its own builder.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@EntryPoint @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
interface LegacyDeps { fun api(): Api; fun prefs(): Prefs }

@Component(dependencies = [LegacyDeps::class], modules = [CheckoutModule::class])
@CheckoutScope interface CheckoutComponent {
    @Component.Builder interface B { fun deps(d: LegacyDeps): B; fun build(): CheckoutComponent }
}
// build: DaggerCheckoutComponent.builder()
//   .deps(EntryPoints.get(app, LegacyDeps::class.java)).build()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Big-bang migration with no green builds in between.
  • Duplicate bindings because the aggregator module and Hilt modules both define them.
  • Treating @Singleton vs a custom @AppScope as the same without alias.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you keep both worlds running at once? → Entry points bridge Hilt to legacy components.
  2. What replaces dagger.android injectors? → @AndroidEntryPoint.
  3. How do you prove behavior unchanged? → Characterization tests and a canary release.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "annotate and delete component". Senior: stages, coexistence rules, shared Activity component conflicts, rollout plan.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Per-Activity binding conflicts surfaced as DuplicateBindings only after the third Activity migrated.

questions.promptHtml: How does @AndroidEntryPoint actually inject an Activity? Walk through what gets generated and the runtime path.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Demonstrates you know it is not magic and can debug generated code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Hilt generates a base class Hilt_MyActivity that extends the original superclass; the Gradle plugin rewrites MyActivity's superclass to it. In onCreate (before super.onCreate's body continues) it asks a ActivityComponentManager for the ActivityComponent, which is built from the retained component held in a ViewModel-like store, then calls the generated MyActivity_GeneratedInjector.injectMyActivity.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
App: Hilt_App.onCreate -> SingletonComponent (generated DaggerApp_HiltComponents_SingletonC)
Activity.onCreate -> Hilt_MyActivity.inject() -> ActivityComponentManager
   -> ActivityRetainedComponentManager (stored in a ViewModelStore => survives rotation)
   -> builds ActivityComponent child -> injects @Inject fields

ActivityRetained survives configuration changes because it is held in a ViewModel inside the Activity's ViewModelStore (implementation detail; verify). One merged component class (HiltComponents) holds all subcomponents; each Hilt module and entry point is aggregated by processors (@AggregatedDeps-style metadata) so the root processor can see them. Without the plugin you must extend Hilt_ classes by hand.

Debugging: read build/generated/ksp/.../Hilt_* and DaggerApp_HiltComponents_SingletonC; error output names the component path ("... is bound in SingletonC ... requested in ActivityC").

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Without the plugin (disabled via hilt { enableAggregatingTask... } or manual)
@AndroidEntryPoint(ComponentActivity::class)
class MainActivity : Hilt_MainActivity()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing work in super.onCreate ordering assumptions: fields are injected at start of onCreate; using them in constructors or property initializers is null/lateinit crash.
  • Thinking injected Activity fields are re-injected after rotation: yes, new Activity, new injection, same retained component.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't injected fields be private? → Generated injector sets them from another class.
  2. Where do Fragments get injected? → In onAttach via the host's component.
  3. Why "Hilt requires the Application to be a Hilt app"? → Component manager walks up to application component.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Hilt generates code". Senior: names the generated artifacts, retained component storage, and uses them to debug.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Using an injected field in a property initializer crashed lateinit not initialized on cold start.

questions.contextHtml:
Crash dashboard shows LeakCanary (debug) and a 0.4% OOM rate on low-end devices (2 GB RAM, 30% of 1.2M DAU) after a "perf refactor". LeakCanary: GC ROOT static ... SingletonC -> ImageLoader -> mContext -> CheckoutActivity (leaking). Code:

@Singleton
class ImageLoader @Inject constructor(
    @ActivityContext private val context: Context,
    private val cache: BitmapCache,
)
@Module @InstallIn(ActivityComponent::class)
abstract class ImgModule { @Binds abstract fun l(i: ImageLoader): Loader }

The team insists the app "compiled fine".
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug and fix it. Why did it compile, and what else would you check?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use WeakReference" or "call clear in onDestroy": treats the symptom and leaves a lifetime mismatch.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is this the code that shipped, or partial? Hilt generates compile errors for Singleton depending on ActivityContext, so was a custom Dagger path or a mixed-up copy involved? Which Hilt version? Is ImageLoader also used by Workers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the @ActivityContext change or switch to @ApplicationContext; ship hotfix via staged rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) scope/context lifetime mismatch; (b) a second holder (listener) keeping Activity; (c) bitmap cache retention, a red herring since LeakCanary points to context.
  4. How I'd verify: Read the LeakCanary trace; run the build and inspect Hilt error output; grep @ActivityContext in @Singleton/@Inject classes; heap dump comparison.
  5. Root cause: A Singleton can only depend on SingletonComponent bindings. As posted, the class is @Singleton yet installed via an Activity-component @Binds; Hilt rejects @ActivityContext in a Singleton-scoped graph at compile time (scope mismatch / MissingBinding), so the posted snippet would not compile. The likely real state: the team bypassed by passing the Activity manually (for example ImageLoader.init(activity) in a @Singleton holder) or a custom Dagger component. Either way, a process-lifetime object holds an Activity-lifetime Context.
  6. Fix: Short term: @ApplicationContext for the loader and pass view-specific needs per call. Long term: if it must be activity-aware, make it @ActivityScoped with @InstallIn(ActivityComponent).
  7. Prevention: LeakCanary in debug CI (instrumented), a Konsist/lint rule banning @ActivityContext in classes annotated @Singleton, review checklist "scope vs context lifetime".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not wrap in WeakReference (hides lifetime error), not remove scope (loses cache sharing).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if it needs theme attributes from the Activity? → Pass the View/Context at call site or use ActivityScoped.
  • Does @ApplicationContext fix Dialogs? → No; dialogs need an Activity context at call time.
  • Why 2 GB devices only? → Heap pressure; leaks show first where headroom is small.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found two screens' worth of Activity graphs retained per session because a singleton analytics wrapper accepted any Context; a single lint rule closed the class of bug.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests WeakReference only.
  • Hire: identifies lifetime mismatch and moves to application context or matching scope.
  • Strong hire: also notes compile-time guard, adds automated leak and architecture checks, and explains why the dump pointed there.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech-style app (2.5M DAU) supports account switching. After switching from user A to B, 0.02% of sessions (about 500 users/day) briefly see A's balance. Support tickets cite "wrong name for ~2 seconds". Singletons: UserRepository (holds StateFlow<Profile>), BalanceCache (@Singleton, Map<AccountId, Balance>), OkHttp interceptor reading token from SessionStore (@Singleton). Logout clears tokens only. No crash logs. Red herring: the CDN cache-control headers were changed last week.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: cause, fix, how to prevent it structurally.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Clear the cache on logout." Correct but manual, will rot with the next singleton.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does it reproduce with airplane mode on (so not CDN)? Does the stale name appear before the first network response? Did it start with the cache feature release? Are there ViewModels surviving across the switch?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side flag to force cold-start restart on account switch (kill process/relaunch), plus clear known caches in SessionStore.clear().
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) in-memory singleton state outliving the user; (b) ViewModel/ActivityRetained instances reused when the Activity is not finished; (c) disk cache (Room/DataStore) keyed globally; (d) CDN (red herring if airplane repro).
  4. How I'd verify: Repro on a debug build with the memory profiler; list all @Singleton classes with mutable state (Dagger generated SingletonC fields); check Room tables for userId column; LeakCanary for retained user-scoped objects.
  5. Root cause: @Singleton means process-lifetime, not session-lifetime. Account switch replaced a token but not the objects that cached per-user data, so first render pulled A's cached state.
  6. Fix: Short term: a SessionScoped-aware Resettable interface multibound into a Set<Resettable>; SessionManager.logout() iterates it. Long term: model session as a custom @DefineComponent (SessionComponent child of SingletonComponent) holding per-user objects, rebuilt on login, with entry-point access; or full process restart if the graph is too tangled.
  7. Prevention: Unit test that every @Singleton with state implements Resettable (reflection test or Konsist); key all disk caches by userId; incident runbook.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Custom component adds graph complexity and call-site changes (cf. the Mercari write-up of a nav-entry component); restart is crude but safe. Not rely on ViewModel clearing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Multi-account simultaneous? → Component per account, keyed in a store.
  • Process death mid-switch? → Persist session id; rebuild on start.
  • Use @ActivityRetainedScoped instead? → No; lives with Activity, not user.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team had eleven singletons caching user data; the multibound reset set found three they had forgotten, one a prefetch queue sending the old token's requests.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: clears one cache and moves on.
  • Hire: identifies scope vs session mismatch and adds a reset mechanism.
  • Strong hire: proposes session component or restart trade-off, structural test, and incident learnings.

questions.contextHtml:
After migrating from a hand-rolled WorkerFactory to Hilt, a sync job that ran fine in debug fails in release for 100% of new installs (~40k/day). Logcat: java.lang.NoSuchMethodException: SyncWorker.<init> [class android.content.Context, class androidx.work.WorkerParameters] and Could not instantiate com.app.SyncWorker. Unit tests green. Code:

@HiltWorker
class SyncWorker @AssistedInject constructor(
    @Assisted ctx: Context, @Assisted p: WorkerParameters, private val repo: SyncRepo
) : CoroutineWorker(ctx, p)
@HiltAndroidApp
class App : Application() { @Inject lateinit var f: HiltWorkerFactory }

Red herring: R8 was updated the same week.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a ProGuard keep rule for the worker." Hides the real wiring gap.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does debug use the same manifest? Is WorkManagerInitializer still in the merged manifest? Is androidx.hilt:hilt-compiler on the processor path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a build with the config fixed; meanwhile fall back to a periodic foreground sync trigger.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Application does not implement Configuration.Provider so WorkManager uses the default factory that needs a no-arg-style constructor; (b) default initializer not removed; (c) missing androidx.hilt compiler so no assisted factory is generated; (d) R8 (red herring: the exception names the constructor signature, not a missing class).
  4. How I'd verify: Inspect the merged manifest (app/build/intermediates/merged_manifests); look for generated SyncWorker_AssistedFactory; adb shell dumpsys jobscheduler; test with WorkManagerTestInitHelper and HiltWorkerFactory.
  5. Root cause: The Application injects the factory but never hands it to WorkManager, and the default initializer builds WorkManager first with the default factory. The default factory reflectively looks for a (Context, WorkerParameters) constructor, which the assisted-inject class does not expose in that form.
  6. Fix: Implement Configuration.Provider, return Configuration.Builder().setWorkerFactory(factory), and remove androidx.work.WorkManagerInitializer via tools:node="remove" on the startup metadata entry (not the whole provider). Ensure ksp("androidx.hilt:hilt-compiler:...") (version per docs 1.4.0 at time of reading; verify).
  7. Prevention: An instrumented test enqueueing the worker with the real factory; CI check on merged manifest.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not keep a custom reflective factory beside Hilt; not remove the entire InitializationProvider.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did debug work? → Possibly a debug-only manifest or an earlier on-demand init path; verify merged manifests per variant.
  • Need a scoped repo in the worker? → Only @Singleton or unscoped.
  • Multi-process app? → Each process builds its own graph; confirm which process runs work.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team lost a week of background sync for new installs because only the debug variant's manifest had been edited.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames R8.
  • Hire: finds missing config and initializer.
  • Strong hire: verifies merged manifest, adds regression test, notes scope limits.

questions.contextHtml: A 140-module app (about 1.8M lines) has 11-minute clean builds and 3.5-minute incremental builds after changing one @Provides in a leaf feature. Build scan shows: kaptReleaseKotlin 25 modules averaging 40s, app module kaptDebugKotlin 95s, hiltAggregateDepsDebug 20s, and many modules with api(project(...)) edges. The team wants "remove Hilt" but leadership wants a measured plan within two weeks.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do, in order, and what savings do you expect?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Drop Hilt for Koin" or "just add more CI machines": no measurement, big blast radius.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is build cache/config cache on? Which Gradle/AGP/Kotlin versions (KSP2 maturity)? What fraction of modules use Hilt? CI vs local pain?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable Gradle build and configuration cache, bump JVM/Gradle heap, remote cache for CI.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) kapt stub generation dominates; (b) api edges widen recompilation and invalidate the app's Dagger pass; (c) giant modules force whole-graph regeneration; (d) Hilt is a minor share compared to Room/Moshi codegen.
  4. How I'd verify: --scan and compare per-task time; -Pandroid.experimental... not needed. Use ./gradlew :app:dependencies; count api edges; make a one-line change and observe task graph for invalidation.
  5. Root cause: kapt in 25 modules (25 x 40s = 1000s of serial-ish cost, parallelizable only partly) plus api edges widening the invalidated set, plus single app-level pass.
  6. Fix: Short term: migrate Hilt/Room/Moshi to KSP module by module (docs show ksp("...hilt-android-compiler")); keep aggregating task on (default; replaces classpath aggregation). Convert api to implementation. Long term: split modules with only @Inject constructors (they don't need Hilt processors in every module if no Hilt modules or entry points, verify), cap the app module, adopt convention plugins.
  7. Prevention: Track task times in CI with Develocity/build scans; dependency-guard; budgets per PR.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rewrite DI; replacing Hilt with Koin moves cost to runtime and loses compile-time validation. Expected gain I would only claim after a pilot of 5 modules (illustrative: if kapt to KSP cuts a module 40s -> about 15s, 25 modules save about 625s of CPU, not necessarily wall time).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can I skip Hilt in feature modules? → Yes when they only use constructor-injected classes and modules live elsewhere, verify aggregation behavior.
  • CI only slow? → Remote cache and incremental test selection.
  • KSP broke on one lib? → Keep that module on kapt, isolate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team halved incremental time by fixing three api edges before touching processors at all.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: proposes removing DI.
  • Hire: measures with scans, moves to KSP.
  • Strong hire: sequences with pilots, quantifies, guards regressions, explains aggregation.

questions.contextHtml:
A UI test passes alone but fails in CI with lateinit property repo has not been initialized for 6 of 120 tests, roughly 5%. Code:

@HiltAndroidTest
@UninstallModules(RepoModule::class)
class CartTest {
    @get:Rule val compose = createAndroidComposeRule<HiltTestActivity>()
    @get:Rule val hilt = HiltAndroidRule(this)
    @Inject lateinit var repo: CartRepo
    @BindValue @JvmField val clock: Clock = FakeClock()
    @Before fun init() { repo.add(Item("a")) }
}

Also a FakeRepoModule with @TestInstallIn(replaces = [RepoModule::class]) exists in the same source set.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and why is it flaky?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a sleep / retry the test."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does failure depend on test order or JVM sharing? Does the compile give warnings? Which rule order is used?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Quarantine the 6 tests, unblock CI.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) rule order: compose rule runs before the Hilt rule; (b) hiltRule.inject() never called; (c) @UninstallModules of a module also replaced by @TestInstallIn; (d) CI emulator slowness (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify: Check docs ordering rule: HiltAndroidRule must be order = 0; read the stack: lateinit accessed in @Before before inject().
  5. Root cause: repo.add is called before hilt.inject() populates @Inject fields, so repo is uninitialized (it is order-independent in all runs; it looks flaky only where some tests don't touch repo early). The mixed @UninstallModules plus @TestInstallIn for the same module is also a conflict: @UninstallModules cannot uninstall @TestInstallIn modules, and the module is replaced twice.
  6. Fix: Order the rules (order = 0 for Hilt), call hilt.inject() first in @Before, drop @UninstallModules and rely on the global @TestInstallIn.
  7. Prevention: Base test class holding the Hilt rule chain; lint/review checklist; run tests with random order locally.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: @UninstallModules per class is slower (extra components), so only for true per-test variation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why @JvmField on @BindValue? → Hilt needs a non-private field, not a Kotlin property getter.
  • Need different fakes per test? → @BindValue with mutable fake reset in @Before.
  • Robolectric differences? → Needs HiltTestApplication configuration via @Config.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team's flaky-test dashboard showed the top offender was a rule-order mistake copied into 30 tests.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds waits.
  • Hire: spots order and missing inject.
  • Strong hire: also catches the double replacement and build-time cost of @UninstallModules.

questions.contextHtml: A checkout flow has 4 screens in one nav graph and 5 ViewModels that must share a CheckoutDraft (cart, address, payment) with stale-free lifetime: created on entering the flow, dropped on exit or on "Done". Today it is @Singleton, so a user who abandons and re-enters sees the old draft (support: 1.1% of checkouts). Single-activity, Navigation Compose, 800k DAU.
questions.promptHtml: What are your options, and which do you choose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make it @ViewModelScoped" (each VM gets its own instance, so nothing is shared) or "clear it manually in onCleared".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must it survive process death? Do ViewModels outside checkout read it? Is the flow ever nested? How much boilerplate will the team accept?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reset CheckoutDraft on flow entry (cheap guard for stale state).
  3. Hypotheses (options), ranked: (a) a CheckoutViewModel scoped to the nav graph entry, other VMs read it via hiltViewModel(parentEntry) or a shared state holder; (b) a custom @DefineComponent scoped to the nav entry (as one team documented with a NavEntryComponent child of ActivityRetainedComponent, a component store keyed by screen id, and a bridge module in ViewModelComponent); (c) keep @Singleton with explicit reset; (d) @ActivityRetainedScoped: nearly the same as Singleton in single-activity, not a fix.
  4. How I'd verify: Prototype (a) first; test enter/abandon/re-enter; Dagger errors on the bridge; heap dump to confirm the draft is collectable after exit.
  5. Root cause: No Hilt scope matches "per navigation flow"; @Singleton/@ActivityRetainedScoped outlive it and @ViewModelScoped is narrower.
  6. Fix: Choose (a): a nav-graph-scoped ViewModel owns the draft and exposes it; it dies with the graph's back stack entry. Use SavedStateHandle for fields that must survive process death. Reserve (b) for when many injected collaborators need the shared state, accepting that every call site moves to a custom ViewModel getter and the graph gets harder to reason about.
  7. Prevention: Test of re-entry; rule "flow state belongs to a flow owner".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not custom component by default: boilerplate, bridge modules, unfamiliar to new hires.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two checkouts at once? → Key by entry id; custom component store handles it, singletons cannot.
  • Navigation 3? → ViewModels scope to NavEntry through the entry decorator, verify API.
  • Test it? → Hilt test plus nav test rule asserting a new instance per entry.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team spent a sprint on a custom component, then replaced it with a graph-scoped ViewModel that deleted 600 lines.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks a scope that cannot express the lifetime.
  • Hire: nav-graph ViewModel with reset.
  • Strong hire: lays out all options, costs of custom components, and chooses with evidence.

questions.contextHtml:
A new :feature:wishlist:impl module is merged. ./gradlew :app:assembleDebug fails:

error: [Dagger/MissingBinding] com.app.wishlist.WishlistRepo cannot be provided without an @Provides-annotated method.
  com.app.wishlist.WishlistRepo is injected at WishlistViewModel(repo)
  WishlistViewModel is injected at ViewModelC ... ProvidesHiltViewModelMap

WishlistRepoImpl has @Inject constructor, and a @Module abstract class WishlistModule { @Binds ... } exists with no @InstallIn. Red herring: a recent Kotlin upgrade.
questions.promptHtml: Fix it and explain how you read Hilt errors in general.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add @Provides in the app module": works, breaks the module boundary.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the :impl a dependency of :app? Does the module apply the Hilt plugin and compiler? Any @Qualifier mismatch?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed beyond unblocking the branch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) missing @InstallIn on the module so Hilt never sees it; (b) module not on app's classpath; (c) KSP/Hilt compiler missing in :impl; (d) Kotlin upgrade (unlikely, the error is a graph error).
  4. How I'd verify: Read the error from the bottom: the dependency path says who requests the type and which component (ViewModelC). Check the module annotation; ./gradlew :app:dependencies | grep wishlist.
  5. Root cause: A @Module without @InstallIn is not part of any Hilt component, so WishlistRepo has no binding in ViewModelC.
  6. Fix: @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class) on the module (and the :app dependency on :impl).
  7. Prevention: Lint or Konsist rule "every @Module has @InstallIn"; a convention plugin applying the Hilt compiler.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not duplicate bindings in :app.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Error says "bound multiple times"? → Two modules bind the same key (typically a duplicate across api/impl).
  • "Expected @HiltAndroidApp"? → Application class missing annotation or wrong Gradle module compiling it.
  • Cycle error? → Break with Provider/Lazy or redesign the dependency.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team added a Konsist test requiring @InstallIn, which caught 7 orphaned modules.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: patches in :app.
  • Hire: adds @InstallIn and reads the path.
  • Strong hire: also prevents recurrence with architecture tests.

questions.contextHtml: Two apps share a 90-module monorepo with a hand-written Dagger setup: AppComponent, ActivityComponent per Activity (23 Activities), a UserComponent subcomponent for logged-in state, and dagger.android fragments. Release train is every 2 weeks, 4M DAU, crash-free target 99.8%. The company wants Hilt in one quarter. Constraints: no feature freeze, rollback possible per release.
questions.promptHtml: Lay out the migration plan and risks.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Do it in one big PR over a weekend."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which Activities have bespoke component arguments? How is UserComponent created? What test coverage exists on DI wiring? Can modules in Dagger be reused as-is?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Establish a baseline: crash-free rate, cold start, build time.
  3. Hypotheses (risks), ranked: (a) per-Activity bindings conflict in Hilt's single shared Activity component; (b) UserComponent has no Hilt equivalent; (c) retained fragments; (d) build time growth from aggregation.
  4. How I'd verify: Prototype one leaf Activity first; compare Dagger graph dumps before/after; dependency report.
  5. Root cause: Not an incident, so the "root" is structural: Hilt standardizes the hierarchy and not everything maps.
  6. Fix (plan): Per the official guide: stage 1, @HiltAndroidApp with modules installed in SingletonComponent via a temporary aggregator, legacy interfaces moved to a @EntryPoint; keep dagger.android until the last one migrates. Stage 2, Activities one by one (leaf first), generalizing Activity-specific bindings to FragmentActivity. Stage 3, Fragments. UserComponent becomes a manual subcomponent installed under SingletonComponent or a @DefineComponent. Each stage ships behind a normal release train with the previous stage already in production.
  7. Prevention: Characterization tests for each screen, Dagger graph snapshot diff in CI, canary rollout at 1% -> 10% -> 100%.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No big bang; no new feature in half-migrated screens; don't rewrite scopes during the migration (alias first, rename later).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rollback after stage 2? → Hilt and Dagger coexist, so revert only the stage's commits.
  • Retained fragment state? → Move into a ViewModel before migrating.
  • Two apps? → Migrate the app with smaller surface first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite migration stalled for a month on a single Activity whose two variants bound different types to the same key.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big bang.
  • Hire: incremental with Application first.
  • Strong hire: handles custom components, rollout metrics, and stops at coexistence boundaries.

questions.contextHtml: You own an internal "payments SDK" AAR consumed by 3 host apps (two use Hilt, one uses Koin) and a dynamic feature module delivered on demand. The SDK currently uses @AndroidEntryPoint Activities and @InstallIn(SingletonComponent) modules. Host-app teams report: (1) the Koin app cannot consume it; (2) duplicate-binding failures when hosts also define OkHttpClient; (3) the dynamic feature cannot see the host's Hilt modules at runtime.
questions.promptHtml: How would you redesign the SDK's DI approach?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Force all hosts onto Hilt."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the SDK public or internal? Who owns release cadence? Must the SDK be usable without the host's graph?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Document required bindings; rename SDK qualifiers to avoid collisions.
  3. Hypotheses (design options), ranked: (a) SDK has no DI framework in its public API: constructor injection plus an explicit PaymentsSdk.init(config, deps); (b) a private Dagger component inside the SDK with required inputs supplied by the host (component dependencies); (c) keep Hilt but publish an optional :sdk-hilt adapter module with @InstallIn bindings; (d) status quo.
  4. How I'd verify: Sample host apps for each DI choice; binary compatibility check; Dagger duplicate-binding test.
  5. Root cause: Hilt modules in a library are global to the host's graph: they pollute it, collide with host bindings, and assume the host uses Hilt.
  6. Fix: (a)+(c): SDK exposes interfaces and a factory, keeps its internal Dagger graph private (qualified, never installed globally), and provides an optional Hilt adapter module so Hilt hosts get one-line integration. For dynamic features, dependencies come from the host via an entry point interface or service-locator contract the feature queries at runtime (dynamic feature modules can't be seen by the base module's Hilt at build time; verify Hilt support for dynamic features in your version).
  7. Prevention: Contract tests per host type, API dump validation.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Internal Dagger doubles build and size cost in the SDK; don't expose Dagger types publicly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need shared OkHttp from host? → Accept an interface in config.
  • Minification? → Ship consumer ProGuard rules for generated classes.
  • Versioning? → Semantic versions; no leaking generated types.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite SDK removed its Hilt modules after two hosts hit conflicting @Singleton bindings, cutting integration time from days to an hour.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: mandates Hilt everywhere.
  • Hire: separates SDK API from DI choice.
  • Strong hire: private graph, adapter module, dynamic feature caveat, versioning.

questions.contextHtml: Cold start p50 rose from 0.9s to 1.8s (p95 2.9s) after adding Hilt-injected initializers. Systrace shows Application.onCreate 700 ms: Hilt_App.onCreate builds the singleton component, then @Inject lateinit var tasks: Set<StartupTask> constructs 22 initializers (Room open, Firebase, a 150 ms crypto key setup, an OkHttp with cache). Device mix: 35% low-end. Play vitals flags excessive startup.
questions.promptHtml: What do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Hilt is slow; remove it."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which initializers are needed before first frame? Is Baseline Profile in use? Are some already on a background thread?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Defer non-critical initializers after first frame.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) eager construction of everything via the Set; (b) a few heavy constructors (crypto, Room open); (c) component creation overhead itself (usually small: generated code, no reflection); (d) class loading on low-end devices.
  4. How I'd verify: Perfetto/Systrace with custom trace sections, Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric, reportFullyDrawn, per-initializer timing.
  5. Root cause: Dependency construction happens where it is requested; injecting Set<StartupTask> into the Application constructs all 22 on the main thread during onCreate. Hilt only moved the work, it did not create it.
  6. Fix: Inject Set<Provider<StartupTask>> or Lazy, classify by phase (critical, after-first-frame, idle), run background-safe ones on a worker dispatcher, make heavy ones lazy at first use, add Baseline Profiles. Keep Room/OkHttp as lazy singletons accessed from background.
  7. Prevention: Startup Macrobenchmark in CI with a budget; trace sections per initializer.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Lazy init moves cost to first use (jank risk on that screen); don't thread-hop things with ordering dependencies without declaring them.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is Hilt itself measurable? → Compare an empty app with and without Hilt using Macrobenchmark; verify instead of assuming.
  • ContentProvider-based init? → Runs before Application.onCreate; avoid graph access there.
  • Multi-process? → Each process pays; limit init per process.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team recovered 600 ms by turning four eager singletons into lazy providers and moving a crypto init off the main thread.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames Hilt without measuring.
  • Hire: lazy/deferred injection with trace evidence.
  • Strong hire: phases initializers, benchmarks in CI, discusses first-use jank trade-off.
